title: Lavender Tallow Balm: The Weird Beef Fat Stuff That Fixed My Spring Skin
body:
Okay so. I was just sitting here, it’s like 8 PM, and I’m putting this stuff on my hands. My cat is judging me from the arm of the couch. The stuff is this whipped tallow balm, lavender scent. Beef tallow. Like, fat. From a cow. You put it on your skin. I know how it sounds. Just wait.

I didn’t go looking for this. My grandma, she’s from the countryside here, she’d mention things. “We used what we had.” Lard for cooking, sure, but other stuff too. For leather, for chapped skin in the barn. I never really listened. Then my skin last winter was a disaster. All red, tight, itchy. Like I was wearing a sweater made of sandpaper. I tried the expensive stuff in the fancy jars. Felt nice going on, did nothing. So I fell down one of those internet holes. You know the ones. You start looking for “dry skin fix” and three hours later you’re reading about traditional tallow skincare from like, the 1800s. That’s where I found it. This whole beef tallow history thing. People have been using animal fats on their skin forever. Not just here, everywhere. Then it got weird and industrial and everyone wanted mineral oil and petroleum jelly. And now? It’s coming back. A natural skincare comeback, I guess. Because the old stuff… sometimes it just works.

## How I Ended Up Putting Cow Fat on My Face

Look, I was skeptical. Very. The idea of rubbing rendered beef suet into my face made me pause. I’m not a homesteader. I buy my milk from the store. But the logic, when you read it, is stupid simple. Our skin’s natural oil, sebum? It has a certain makeup. Tallow from grass-fed cows is apparently really close to that. Closer than any plant oil or lab-made thing. So it’s like your skin recognizes it. It absorbs. It doesn’t just sit there like a greasy film. This particular balm is whipped, made in France, feels… luxurious isn’t the right word. That’s a marketing word. It feels substantial. Kind of waxy when you scoop it, but then it melts from your fingers. Weird.

I ordered the lavender one because spring here is a liar. It’s sunny but the wind is still sharp, and my anxiety does this fun little spike when the seasons change. They said calming, sleep-promoting. I figured if it didn’t help my skin, maybe it’d chill me out. The jar showed up. Small. Simple. I opened it. Smelled like lavender. Not fake candle lavender, not perfume. More like… dried lavender in an old linen cupboard. Herbal. Timeless, maybe. That’s the word they used. It fits. It’s a night cream for me. A ritual. Wash face, slap on some of this, try to convince my brain to shut off.

## What This Lavender Tallow Balm Actually Does (Or What It Did For Me)

So the first night I used it, I just did my face. Felt rich. I went to bed expecting to wake up a greaseball. I didn’t. My skin just felt… quiet. Not tight. Not angry. Just skin. That was new.

But the real test was my hands. I get these cracks in spring, right on the knuckles. From the cold, from washing, from existing. Painful. Look terrible. I started slathering this tallow balm on them at night. Like, a lot. Put on some old cotton socks as gloves. Felt ridiculous. Woke up. The cracks weren’t gone, but they were softer. Less red. After three nights? Basically healed. I was stunned. I have a tube of prescription cream that didn’t work that fast. For rough hands, for winter damage that’s lingering into spring? This stuff is a secret weapon. I read it’s good for psoriasis too. I don’t have that, but I get it now. It’s like giving your skin what it’s actually asking for, not what some chemist thinks it should want.

Here’s a random detail: the jar lives on my bedside table now. There’s a faint ring on the wood from where I put it down with damp fingers. That’s how often I use it. It’s just there. Part of the routine.

## My Skin After a Few Weeks of This Weirdness

I’m not gonna say I look 20 again. That’s stupid. But my skin is… calmer. The constant low-level irritation I didn’t even fully notice until it was gone? Gone. It’s more resilient. I can go outside in that sneaky spring wind and my cheeks don’t scream. My elbows, which are always a disaster, are actually presentable. It’s a subtle thing. It’s not a “glow.” It’s just health. Like my skin barrier isn’t freaking out all the time trying to protect itself.

I told my mom about it. She laughed. Then she tried it on her gardening hands. Now she wants a jar. The circle is complete, I guess. Grandma’s vague memories, my internet rabbit hole, mom’s dry hands. It’s all connected by this stupidly simple thing: tallow.

I got mine from this little Etsy shop. No fancy branding. Just the facts. Grass-fed, whipped, French-made. It feels honest. In a world of a million serums with unpronounceable ingredients, that honesty is kind of refreshing. And it works. I’m on my second jar now. I’ll probably order another soon because I’m paranoid about running out.

## Quick Questions I Get Asked

**Is beef tallow good for your face?**
Yeah, surprisingly. The science-y reason is that its fat profile is really similar to our own skin’s sebum. So it absorbs deeply and helps reinforce your skin barrier instead of just coating it. It sounds medieval, but it makes biological sense.

**Does tallow balm clog pores?**
It hasn’t for me, and I can get clogged pores. Because it’s so similar to our own oils, it seems to absorb properly. It doesn’t feel like it’s sitting on top of my skin suffocating it like some heavy creams do. It just… sinks in.

**What does the lavender tallow balm smell like?**
It’s a calm, herbal lavender. Not sweet. Not like air freshener. More like dried lavender buds. It’s relaxing. I use it as part of my wind-down before bed and the scent really helps with that. It’s not overpowering, just… there.

Anyway. That’s my experience. If your skin is feeling angry, tight, or just generally misunderstood with the season change, this traditional approach might be worth a shot. I was skeptical too. Now the jar on my nightstand with the little water ring is just proof that sometimes, the old ways come back for a reason. It just works.
